slides.title: Principle and place of the method
bullets: Sedimentation goes through three phases: first the red cells settle singly and slowly, then they form aggregates and settle fast, in the third phase the aggregates pack down and settling slows and stops.
ESR is not specific to any disease: it is used as a preliminary test and a screening test.

The Aripova book notes that ESR is not specific for finding acute and chronic diseases, is little used today and has been abandoned in many countries: age, pregnancy, the phase of the cycle and anaemia distort the result.

slides.title: Principle and place of the method
bullets: The international committee for standardisation and WHO recommend venous blood, an anticoagulant tube and a graduated vertical tube (the Westergren principle).

slides.title: Limitations and errors
bullets: ESR is not suitable when the red-cell count is reduced or the patient is dehydrated.
Physiological factors (age, pregnancy, phase of the menstrual cycle) and anaemia can give a wrong result.
The value may be raised in diseases that change the plasma protein pattern, chronic infection, normal pregnancy, tumours and tuberculosis.
The capillary-blood, 100 mm tube method used in laboratories of the former USSR should, where possible, be revised to meet international standards.

slides.title: C-reactive protein (CRP)
slides.eyebrow: Proteins and inflammation · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (serum)  ·  Units: mg/dL

What it is used for: CRP shows how much inflammation is present in the body. It is ordered with symptoms of a bacterial infection (fever or chills, rapid heart rate, rapid breathing, nausea and vomiting), to check for a chronic inflammatory condition, to monitor for infection after surgery, to follow a condition and its treatment, and to help make treatment decisions in sepsis.
CRP rises and falls with the amount of inflammation, so a falling CRP suggests that treatment is working or that the body is healing on its own.

slides.title: C-reactive protein (CRP)
slides.eyebrow: Proteins and inflammation · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: CRP is made by the liver in response to inflammation. Short-lived acute inflammation helps tissues heal from injury or infection, whereas long-lasting (chronic) inflammation can damage healthy tissue; it is most often caused by autoimmune disorders, but also by repeated injury or irritation, for example from smoking.

slides.title: C-reactive protein (CRP)
slides.eyebrow: Proteins and inflammation · Interpreting the result
bullets: High: High CRP may indicate an acute or chronic condition, such as bacterial or viral infections, inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis), autoimmune disorders (lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, vasculitis) or lung diseases such as asthma. Smoking and exposure to environmental toxins, such as polluted air, can also raise CRP.

High: Healthy people usually have very low CRP, and any increase may mean inflammation. Increases have also been linked to insomnia, depression, hormone therapy for menopause and obesity, and females often have slightly higher CRP than males.

slides.title: C-reactive protein (CRP)
slides.eyebrow: Proteins and inflammation · Pre-analytics and interferences
bullets: Interferences: Some medicines and supplements may affect the result; tell the provider about everything taken, including magnesium and NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and aspirin. Prescription medicines should not be stopped without talking with the provider.
Limitations: CRP shows how much inflammation there is, but not its cause or location. A diagnosis requires other test results, symptoms and medical history.
A standard CRP test should not be confused with a high-sensitivity CRP (hs-CRP) test. Both measure CRP, but hs-CRP detects very small increases and is used to estimate the risk of heart disease.

slides.title: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (tube type per laboratory instructions)

What it is used for: ESR is used with other tests to help diagnose and monitor conditions that cause inflammation, such as arthritis, vasculitis, infections and inflammatory bowel diseases (ulcerative colitis and Crohn’s disease).
It is ordered for symptoms of inflammation: headaches, unexplained fever or weight loss, joint stiffness, neck or shoulder pain, loss of appetite, anemia.

slides.title: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: Red blood cells normally sink slowly. Inflammation makes them stick together in clumps, which are heavier than single cells and sink faster. Blood is placed in a tall, thin tube and the speed of settling is measured: faster rates mean more inflammation.

slides.title: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result
bullets: High: A high ESR (red cells sank faster than normal) may come from inflammatory conditions such as giant cell arteritis, arthritis, systemic vasculitis, polymyalgia rheumatica, inflammatory bowel disease, kidney disease, infections, rheumatoid arthritis and other autoimmune diseases, heart disease and certain cancers.

Low: A low ESR (red cells sank slower than normal) may be caused by blood disorders such as polycythemia, sickle cell disease or very high leukocytosis, heart failure and certain kidney and liver problems.

slides.title: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/2
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for this test. If other tests are ordered on the same blood sample, fasting (no food or drink) for several hours may be required.

Interferences: Normal ESR varies with age and sex. Pregnancy, the menstrual cycle, aging, obesity, drinking alcohol regularly and exercise can affect results, as can certain medicines and supplements — tell the provider about them.

slides.title: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/2
bullets: Limitations: ESR alone cannot diagnose which condition is causing inflammation, and it is possible to have an inflammatory condition with a normal ESR. A C-reactive protein (CRP) test is commonly done with it to provide more information.

slides.title: Rheumatoid arthritis
bullets: With rheumatoid arthritis symptoms, lab results are judged with symptoms and a physical exam: RF and anti-CCP are interpreted together.
